title: The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky

teacherSummary.text: Marshal Jack Potter rides a Pullman car home to Yellow Sky with his new bride, anxious because he married without telling the town. Meanwhile drunken Scratchy Wilson terrorizes the empty street with revolvers, looking for his old enemy Potter. Scratchy confronts the unarmed marshal, hears he is married, says 'I s'pose it's all off now,' and walks away.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky,” how does Crane show the closing of the frontier? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky, how does Crane develop the idea of the closing of the frontier? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky develops the idea of the closing of the frontier. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of the closing of the frontier. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky suggests about the closing of the frontier. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's irony and setting), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Stephen Crane uses irony in The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky to complicate the reader's understanding of the closing of the frontier. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the closing of the frontier responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the closing of the frontier follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky and its treatment of the closing of the frontier. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's irony and setting, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky as evidence for a larger claim about the closing of the frontier in The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the closing of the frontier. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky.

satQuestions.passage: The bride was not pretty, nor was she very young. She wore a dress of blue cashmere, with small reservations of velvet here and there and with steel buttons abounding. middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Gunplay; drunkenness. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
